findings.title: Backup code consumption is not atomic (read-modify-write race)
findings.body: In the credentials authorize() handler, the backup code list is read from the DB, matched, set to null, and written back with prisma.user.update. Two concurrent login attempts using the same backup code can both pass the indexOf check before either write lands, so a single-use code can be replayed and used twice (or more). The update should be conditional/atomic (e.g., compare-and-set in a transaction, or store per-code hash and delete with a WHERE clause that asserts the code still exists).

findings.title: Backup code is consumed before the login flow completes
findings.body: The verified backup code is deleted and the DB updated inside authorize(), before next-auth issues the session/JWT and before the signIn callback runs. If anything downstream fails (signIn callback error, network failure on the client, next-auth internal error), the user's backup code is permanently burned without a successful login, reducing their remaining recovery codes through no fault of their own. Ideally consumption should happen only once login is certain to succeed.

findings.title: Backup codes unusable for third-party identity provider (SAML/Google) 2FA users
findings.body: The check `if (user.identityProvider !== IdentityProvider.CAL && !credentials.totpCode) throw ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` runs before the backup code branch. Users whose accounts use SAML/Google identity but have 2FA enabled (the totp-link login path) can never authenticate with a backup code: submitting a backupCode without a totpCode always throws, and the login page's 'Lost access' backup-code UI is not offered on the totpEmail path either. These users have no recovery option if they lose their authenticator, despite the feature claiming to provide one.

findings.title: No test for the core feature: logging in with a backup code
findings.body: The PR adds backup-code login and backup-code-based 2FA disable, but the only new test coverage clicks the download/copy/close buttons on the setup screen (and even that doesn't verify file or clipboard content). There is no test that a user can actually log in with a backup code, that a used code is rejected on reuse, that an incorrect code shows the right error, or that disabling 2FA with a backup code works — all explicitly deferred as TODOs. The primary security-relevant code path ships untested.

findings.title: Both totpCode and backupCode can be submitted; backup code silently takes precedence
findings.body: When switching between the TOTP and 'Lost access' backup-code views, only one field is cleared in some transitions, and onSubmit spreads all form values into signIn(). The authorize() handler checks backupCode first, so a user who has a stale backupCode value in the form while trying to log in with a TOTP code will get an 'incorrect backup code' error (or worse, succeed via a leftover backup code) even though they typed a valid TOTP. The submit should send only the code relevant to the currently active mode.

findings.title: Backup codes are generated and persisted before 2FA is actually enabled
findings.body: The setup endpoint writes encrypted backupCodes to the user row on every call, even if the user never completes the enable step. A user who starts setup, sees/saves codes, then restarts setup later and completes only the second attempt will have the first set of saved codes silently invalidated (overwritten). Also, codes exist on the DB for users who never enabled 2FA. Generating/persisting codes only on successful enable (or returning them from enable) would make the displayed codes authoritative.
